summary: Liberal theology is the modern, chiefly nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century, Protestant movement descending from Friedrich Schleiermacher and developed by Albrecht Ritschl and Adolf von Harnack, that sought to reconcile Christianity with modern thought by grounding it in religious experience and ethics, embracing the historical-critical study of the Bible, and emphasizing the moral teaching and the person of Jesus over inherited dogma. In the early twentieth century it met a sharp reaction, above all the dialectical or crisis theology of Karl Barth after the First World War.
description:
Liberal theology (also called liberal Protestantism or Protestant liberalism) is the broad movement in modern Protestant thought, running chiefly through the nineteenth and into the early twentieth century, that undertook to reconcile the Christian faith with modern knowledge and culture. Historians of doctrine standardly trace its lineage from Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834), who relocated the ground of religion from doctrine and metaphysics to immediate religious experience, and follow its development through Albrecht Ritschl (1822-1889), who centred theology on the kingdom of God, moral community, and value-judgments rather than metaphysical speculation, to Ritschl's pupil Adolf von Harnack (1851-1930), the historian of dogma whose Berlin lectures What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums, 1900) gave the movement one of its most widely read statements.

As surveyed by Claude Welch and by Gary Dorrien, several commitments recur across the movement's varied forms: a grounding of religion in experience and in ethics rather than in inherited orthodoxy; the acceptance of the historical-critical study of the Bible and of the results of modern science and philosophy; an emphasis on the moral teaching of Jesus and on the person of Jesus over against speculative or dogmatic construction; and, in many of its representatives, a confidence in moral and cultural progress that critics later named cultural Protestantism (Kulturprotestantismus). In Harnack's own account the essence of the Gospel could be summarized under three heads, 'Firstly, the kingdom of God and its coming. Secondly, God the Father and the infinite value of the human soul. Thirdly, the higher righteousness and the commandment of love.'

Against this movement came a sharp reaction in the early twentieth century. Karl Barth (1886-1968), trained in the liberal theology of his day, broke with it after the First World War; the radically rewritten second edition of his commentary The Epistle to the Romans (Der Roemerbrief, 1922) is widely treated as the opening of what is called dialectical or crisis theology, which reasserted the transcendence and otherness of God ('wholly other') and God's self-revelation over against a theology grounded in human religious experience, moral progress, and cultural Christianity. This entry presents both liberal theology's own commitments and Barth's reaction as attributed positions and does not adjudicate between them.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes liberal theology on the terms of its own representatives and of the historians of doctrine who survey it (neutrality #6), and it presents both the movement's characteristic commitments AND Karl Barth's early-twentieth-century reaction against it as attributed positions, adjudicating neither (neutrality #1, #2). The movement's defining commitments (religion grounded in experience and ethics, the historical-critical study of the Bible, the emphasis on the moral teaching and person of Jesus over dogma, and in many forms a confidence in moral and cultural progress) are stated as the movement's account. Barth's dialectical/crisis theology is stated as his attributed reaction, mirroring the refuted edge to friedrich-schleiermacher in the karl-barth entry and the related_to edge to karl-barth in the friedrich-schleiermacher entry. This entry is referenced by friedrich-schleiermacher (whose influenced edge to liberal-theology it closes) and by karl-barth.

Sourcing triangulates the three Christian lenses per neutrality #8: (a) academic historians of doctrine (Claude Welch, Protestant Thought in the Nineteenth Century; Gary Dorrien, The Making of American Liberal Theology); (b) an open primary, Adolf von Harnack's What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums), the movement's own voice; (c) a contemporary theologian on the movement and its critique (Alister E. McGrath). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources.

CONFIDENCE HONESTY: This entry is REVIEWED-eligible, not verified, and only ONE source is rated high. Harnack's What Is Christianity? in T. B. Saunders's translation (the sixteen lectures delivered at the University of Berlin during the winter-term 1899-1900) was read directly, line by line, in the OPEN, public-domain full text at the Internet Archive (both the archive.org detail page and the plain-text djvu were confirmed to resolve, freely readable, not borrow-only), and the load-bearing passage was verified verbatim: Harnack summarizes the Gospel under three heads, 'Firstly, the kingdom of God and its coming. Secondly, God the Father and the infinite value of the human soul. Thirdly, the higher righteousness and the commandment of love.' On the strength of that direct reading the Harnack source is rated HIGH for the claims it backs (the movement's emphasis on the kingdom of God, the fatherhood of God and the value of the human soul, and the moral teaching of Jesus, as stated by one of its central figures). The general characterization of the movement as a whole (its span, its lineage from Schleiermacher through Ritschl, and its recurrent commitments) rests on the secondary scholarship (Welch, Dorrien, McGrath), which is rated MEDIUM: verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher and catalogue records, not read line by line. The dates given (Schleiermacher 1768-1834, Ritschl 1822-1889, Harnack 1851-1930, Barth 1886-1968) are secure and standardly reported.

period.note: Approximate. Conventionally traced from Schleiermacher's On Religion (1799) and The Christian Faith (1821-22), through Albrecht Ritschl (active mid-nineteenth century) and Adolf von Harnack's What Is Christianity? (1900), and standardly said to meet its decisive challenge with Karl Barth's Epistle to the Romans (2nd ed., 1922) after the First World War. Dates mark a long development and a shifting reception rather than a single origin or a clean end; liberal and revisionist Protestant theology continued in various forms through the twentieth century, so no active_until is asserted.

relations.note: Friedrich Schleiermacher (1768-1834) is standardly credited by historians of doctrine as the father of modern liberal Protestant theology, for relocating the ground of religion to immediate religious experience; the movement's later representatives (Ritschl, Harnack) develop from this lineage. Attributed as his contribution and its reception, not endorsed. friedrich-schleiermacher exists in the dataset; this edge closes his influenced edge to liberal-theology.

In the early twentieth century Karl Barth (1886-1968), trained in liberal theology, broke sharply with it; his dialectical/crisis theology, especially the second edition of The Epistle to the Romans (1922), reasserted God's transcendence and self-revelation over against a theology grounded in human religious experience and cultural progress. Recorded as Barth's attributed reaction, not adjudicated; mirrors the refuted edge to friedrich-schleiermacher in the karl-barth entry. karl-barth exists in the dataset.

Adolf von Harnack (1851-1930), historian of dogma and pupil of Ritschl, whose Berlin lectures What Is Christianity? (Das Wesen des Christentums, 1900) gave the movement one of its most widely read statements; the open primary read for this entry. Dangling forward reference, not yet a separate entry.

Albrecht Ritschl (1822-1889), who centred theology on the kingdom of God, moral community, and value-judgments rather than metaphysical speculation, and taught Harnack; a central figure in the movement's development. Dangling forward reference, not yet a separate entry.
